Nice read from Salesforce AI Research and colleagues. There is a lot of interest in self-improving harnesses, but the harness editor is usually a fixed frontier model. JoMoHa trains two policies with RL from the same task outcomes. One writes the executable harness, and the other solves the task inside it. Updating the model and the harness in turns caused trouble. Performance rose and then fell as the two became incompatible. Keeping separate histories and value estimates for each policy fixed that. JoMoHa beat weight-only and harness-only training on ALFWorld, WebShop, and DBBench, averaging 70.3% and reaching 97.0% on ALFWorld. Training the harness writer also beat freezing it. https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.11499 Chat with Paper: https://academy.dair.ai/papers/jomoha-joint-model-harness-optimization-with-reinforcement-learning-2611.11499

A renaissance of software in 2027? Closing talk from @trq212 at @aiDotEngineer in two sentences: 2026 was the industrial revolution of software. Now let’s build its Renaissance. We’ve spent this year obsessing over software factories, coding agents, productivity, and how much software we can produce. And yes, the industrial revolution is happening. Software is becoming dramatically cheaper to build. But Thariq argues something equally exciting is happening: as AI gets better, we no longer have to adapt to how models prefer to work. We can make them work the way WE want. And that opens up an enormous creative frontier. New programming languages designed around human understanding. New databases. New operating systems. New interfaces. Decades of HCI research suddenly worth revisiting. His own experiment is a game where AI handles the complicated engine while he works in a human-readable language he designed to control every creative decision. The point is to stop accepting whatever software AI happens to generate and start shaping what software could actually become. The industrial revolution is about making more things, faster and cheaper. The Renaissance is about making things we couldn’t even conceive of before, with more creativity, quality, and soul. And… the Renaissance won’t happen automatically because models get smarter. We - you - have to build it. That’s a pretty exciting mission for 2027. Great paper on decision models for long-horizon agents. For agent RL, you want the decision model to evaluate completed trajectories and leave action selection to the policy. Decision models output a typed distribution, such as a probability for each option. As actors on ALFWorld, all six models tested (three decision models and three general LLMs) went for an easier subgoal before the one that had to come first. Shown the full trajectory and asked whether each action helped, the same models gave credit to the steps they skipped while acting. Used as a teacher for GRPO, one of the decision models raised a Qwen2.5-1.5B policy from 72.8% to 82.9% success on ALFWorld and from 56.8% to 71.4% on WebShop, including on tasks it rarely completes as an actor. https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.17167 Chat with Paper: https://academy.dair.ai/papers/actor-judge-or-teacher-understanding-decision-models-in-long-horizon-agents-2611.17167

Great paper from Google on building benchmarks for data agents. Static data-agent benchmarks saturate quickly and can't target a specific skill. SynthCorp generates the data instead. It simulates routine business events and disruptions on a virtual calendar, and those events fill relational tables, a document store, and a data catalog that stay consistent with each other. Every operation goes into a simulation log, so the gold answer for each task is derived from the log and checked without manual annotation. The first release has seven data estates with up to 1,000 tables and 256 tasks across five domains. Tasks that chain several business events together still make state-of-the-art agents fail. https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.14765 Chat with Paper: https://academy.dair.ai/papers/synthcorp-a-platform-for-creating-benchmarks-for-data-agents-2611.14765

This short RSI explainer was fully generated by a model. The model is ERNIE 5.5 Flash Preview, Baidu's new model. I gave it one task. "Make a short video that explains recursive self-improvement (RSI)." I used pi as the agent harness and ElevenLabs for the voice. Everything else came from ERNIE, working on its own for about 8 minutes. For the same video, it would take 2x-5x longer with frontier models. I am learning that these flash models can execute these tasks faster and with higher quality than was possible just a couple of months ago. It wrote the code for the loop diagram and the charts. It wrote the script and rendered the final film. This is the long-running agent work Baidu built it for. It's a 280B model with 14B active parameters and a 1M-token context window. I am not testing it with longer videos where coherence matters. Baidu also tuned it for game development in engines like Unreal, Unity, and Godot. For knowledge work, it can plan a task and produce spreadsheets, documents, slide decks, and research reports. It's free on OpenRouter right now. Baidu says the open weights will land before Nov 25. https://openrouter.ai/baidu/ernie-5.5-flash-preview:free Media

Interesting how relevant this 1999 Microsoft Research paper on human-agent interaction has become. The idea isn't new, but it's becoming increasingly important as AI agents grow more autonomous: figuring out when agents should act independently, when they should ask for help, and how humans should intervene. The paper introduces principles for mixed-initiative interfaces, where humans and intelligent agents share control based on uncertainty, context, and the cost of interruptions. Almost three decades later, Antimattr is exploring the hardware side of this problem with AI earphones and a smart ring designed to let people direct agents through voice. As agents become capable of handling longer, more complex workflows, the interface between humans and agents becomes an important part of the system. Worth revisiting this research as we think about the next generation of agent infrastructure. https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/research/publication/principles-mixed-initiative-user-interfaces/ we shut down a software business making $250k a year to build a hardware company put $20k of our own money into it, moved to the US with less than 3 months of runway, and eventually got into @ycombinator today, we're introducing @antimattr_one we're building a voice-first hardwa…

By the way, I have been working on a system that produces these technical visual explainers for papers and talks. Explainers have also become a huge part of how I produce artifacts, which really helps with understanding technical topics. So I got super excited about these results because you often don't want to wait too long for some of these generations. These flash models are very promising for this. I will share more thoughts in a future post on how I use explainers alongside visual artifacts across a wider range of workflows.

Highly recommended read. My notes: I have recently started independent research on co-evolved models. My focus has been on co-evolving models and harnesses. This work focuses on memory writing specifically for continual learning. Why is this a big deal? As you work with an agent, it should get better at your tasks, but that obviously doesn't happen easily, and current external memory systems often aren't enough. This has less to do with memory systems (there are many great ones out there) and more to do with the model's awareness and judgment about when to act. To illustrate, imagine an AI agent spends a week fixing bugs in the same project. We would expect it to learn how the project works and avoid repeating mistakes. Giving it a place to save notes lets it carry that knowledge into later tasks. But choosing what belongs in those notes requires judgment. This work looks at how to train that judgment with RL. They essentially teach an agent to discover useful information while working and write memories that help it succeed on later tasks. A trained 4B parameter model reached a score similar to GPT-5.4 and Claude Opus 4.7. RIME uses one model in two roles. As the actor, it works on a task using its existing memory. As the writer, it reviews what happened and updates the notes available for the next task. The training rewards each role differently. The writer receives credit when performance on the next few tasks improves relative to performance on the recent tasks. This gives it a reason to preserve information that will help later. The comparison is an approximate training signal, since other actions and memory updates also affect those results. The actor earns a reward for completing its task and an additional reward for discoveries that reach memory. An AI judge compares the old and new notes, looking for useful additions, corrected beliefs, and concrete leads. This encourages the agent to investigate enough to learn something reusable. Rewriting the same notes in different words earns little credit. The researchers found that these abilities need to develop together. A writer depends on the information the actor discovers, and an actor depends on the knowledge the writer preserves. One big question I have here is efficiency and, obviously, how it all integrates into harnesses and workflows. I think approaches like this can save a lot of tokens and turns. While this is on a small scale, it's great to see it working already. It feels like a more feasible approach for continual learning. Frontier models are getting better at retaining knowledge, but I think efficient continual learning will still require touching the weights, which is where open-weight models will play a huge role. How can we train LLMs to write memories from experience collected on the fly to as best as possible solve the next task, i.e., optimize for both capability and "continual learning" ability? In our new post, we study this question in the setting continual learning over a sequence…
